comparator.name: Cultural Anthropology and Development Sociology
comparator.sourceNotes: The official pages give 60 EC each year. The first two years comprise all listed required courses (60 EC each); the third has 30 EC compulsory, including a 9-EC thesis and a separate 15-EC independent fieldwork project. For the remaining 30 EC this pathway uses the officially permitted course-choice option at Radboud or elsewhere; the alternative 18-EC work placement plus 12 EC courses is not combined with it. No named formal route is selected. The year-specific pages are indicative 2026–2027 information, not a guaranteed future cohort schedule.

alternatives.label: Closest match to cultural anthropology and development sociology
alternatives.concept: A social and cultural inquiry route linking inequality, cultural meaning, colonial histories, global cooperation and qualitative research. Sociology, history, law and political science provide related perspectives, while UCR does not offer Radboud’s dedicated anthropology sequence or independent ethnographic fieldwork.
alternatives.labelReason: The full curriculum combines social theory, cultural and colonial histories, social justice, research, rights and environmental change; the target-relative label identifies it as the closest feasible response without claiming a full anthropology major.
progression: Introductions to sociology, history, rights and climate precede advanced social theory, Indigenous histories, political study and environmental governance. Qualitative and statistical methods appear before final-year research-related work; formal prerequisites and term availability pass.

alternatives.label: Climate justice and human–nature relations
alternatives.concept: A route examining environmental change through social inequality, Indigenous history, ecological science, sustainability governance and environmental justice. Qualitative social research and media analysis retain the target’s concern with lived perspectives, while specialist anthropological fieldwork remains a Radboud strength.
alternatives.labelReason: A substantial environmental science sequence is linked to sociology, justice and governance rather than appearing as an incidental theme; the title names that actual combination.
alternatives.distinctness: This curriculum substitutes foundations in sustainability and ecology, conservation, Earth-system methods, environmental biogeochemistry and applied environmental research for the broad route’s political institutions, private law, gender history and cultural-media courses. These changes implement the target’s evidenced climate-justice and human–nature direction.
progression: Climate and sustainability foundations precede environmental systems and advanced biogeochemistry; introductory sociology precedes social theory, and introductory biodiversity precedes conservation. All formal prerequisites and planned term offerings pass.

candidates.label: Migration and multicultural belonging
candidates.reason: The target clearly supports this direction, but the current UCR catalogue lacks enough directly relevant advanced study of migration, mobility and lived belonging for a credible distinct 24-course curriculum. Law and political courses would be contextual additions, not a substitute for that sequence.

selection.assessment: The closest feasible response combines cultural meaning, social inequality, global change and related social research. The climate-justice route shifts materially toward human–nature questions with ecological science and environmental governance; the pair differs by more than four courses. Migration and belonging are evidenced, but the current UCR catalogue cannot support a distinct 24-course programme on that direction without making law and politics courses stand in for specialist mobility and ethnographic study.

blocks: Both examine changing gender relations, though UCR treats them primarily through history.
Both use a specific region to study cultural meaning and colonial encounters; UCR focuses on West African heritage.
Both use visual narrative to investigate and communicate people’s experiences; documentary study does not reproduce anthropological arts-based field methods.
Both introduce social structures and inequality; Radboud integrates cultural and development perspectives.
Both examine societal change through sociological theory; Radboud combines this with more sustained anthropology.
Both engage with debates in social theory; Radboud has more dedicated anthropological scholarship.
Both consider international relationships and cooperation; UCR treats the field through political theory.
Both address power and decision-making around society–environment relations; UCR focuses on sustainability governance.
Both develop qualitative inquiry into social experience; UCR’s course is general sociological methodology.
Both use statistical inference in empirical social research, with UCR applying it through psychology and experimental methods.
Both develop reflective academic skills, although Radboud also credits later professional and research elements separately.
The selected UCR courses do not directly study kinship as a sustained anthropological subject.
A course in qualitative methods does not replace Radboud’s separately credited first-year research project.
The UCR statistics course is aligned to the subsequent statistics component; Radboud credits descriptive statistics separately.
UCR’s personal development course is shown elsewhere; this distinct socially engaged component has no direct credited match.
The selected methods course is qualitative but does not independently reproduce the participatory-methods component.
The selected UCR courses do not specifically study debt relations and financial behaviour.
Ethics is present in a UCR alternative, but it does not reproduce a philosophy-of-science course on knowledge and research.
The separate nine-credit participatory research project has no scheduled UCR fieldwork equivalent.
European political institutions provide context, but no included UCR course directly examines lived im/mobility and belonging at this scope.
A stand-alone literature review is not present as an independent credited UCR component.
The second socially engaged learning component is separate from UCR’s first-year PPD.
Radboud’s nine-credit bachelor thesis is required; UCR optional research is a comparison-only option.
Radboud requires fifteen credits of independent fieldwork, which the UCR schedules do not provide.
The thirty-credit Radboud free-choice space remains genuinely open and is not assigned invented courses.

notes.text: Radboud combines anthropology and development sociology with a specialist theory and methods sequence, independent fieldwork and a bachelor thesis. UCR can approach inequality, cultural meaning and human–nature relations through sociology, history, law, media and environmental study, but these courses do not constitute the full disciplinary fieldwork curriculum.
